svg.title: Retained Yield by Merchant Segment and Payment Rail
svg.desc: diagram id: diag-04-retained-payment-rail-yields; chart type: horizontal_bars; title: Retained Yield by Merchant Segment and Payment Rail; subtitle: Illustrative operator dollars retained per 1,000 successful payment events.; chapter number: 2; epistemic tag: illustrative_model; assumptions note: Card examples assume a $50 average ticket. Gateway yield is a separate component, not an additional merchant cohort. ATM events are withdrawals, not purchases; differing event economics prevent direct conclusions about account profitability. Bars are not additive.; caption: Price retained yield after upstream splits, then subtract operator acquisition, servicing, and loss costs.; stages: label: Card-present retail residual; value: $120 retained per 1,000 purchases; numeric value: 120.0; detail: One thousand $50 purchases produce $50,000 merchant volume; a 24-basis-point retained residual produces $120 before operator expenses, without assuming debit surcharges.; label: Restaurant processing residual; value: $160 retained per 1,000 purchases; numeric value: 160.0; detail: A 32-basis-point retained residual on $50,000 merchant volume produces $160; verify tip adjustments, funding timing, terminal support, and rate-matching exposure.; label: Gateway transaction markup; value: $90 retained per 1,000 transactions; numeric value: 90.0; detail: A $0.09 retained gateway markup produces $90 across 1,000 transactions; deduct the upstream gateway charge before measuring this component and avoid residual double counting.; label: Sponsor-approved specialty merchant; value: $250 retained per 1,000 purchases; numeric value: 250.0; detail: A 50-basis-point retained residual on $50,000 merchant volume produces $250. Model reserves, disputes, and service burden separately; higher yield does not establish higher profit.; label: Exclusive-venue ATM withdrawals; value: $1,750 retained per 1,000 withdrawals; numeric value: 1750.0; detail: A $3.00 surcharge less $1.25 combined venue and upstream shares retains $1.75 per withdrawal. Four thousand annual withdrawals retain $7,000 before operator servicing expenses.

text.title: Retained Yield by Merchant Segment and Payment Rail
text.tspan: Retained Yield by Merchant Segment and Payment Rail

circle.title: label: Card-present retail residual; value: $120 retained per 1,000 purchases; numeric value: 120.0; detail: One thousand $50 purchases produce $50,000 merchant volume; a 24-basis-point retained residual produces $120 before operator expenses, without assuming debit surcharges.

label: Restaurant processing residual; value: $160 retained per 1,000 purchases; numeric value: 160.0; detail: A 32-basis-point retained residual on $50,000 merchant volume produces $160; verify tip adjustments, funding timing, terminal support, and rate-matching exposure.

label: Gateway transaction markup; value: $90 retained per 1,000 transactions; numeric value: 90.0; detail: A $0.09 retained gateway markup produces $90 across 1,000 transactions; deduct the upstream gateway charge before measuring this component and avoid residual double counting.

label: Sponsor-approved specialty merchant; value: $250 retained per 1,000 purchases; numeric value: 250.0; detail: A 50-basis-point retained residual on $50,000 merchant volume produces $250. Model reserves, disputes, and service burden separately; higher yield does not establish higher profit.

label: Exclusive-venue ATM withdrawals; value: $1,750 retained per 1,000 withdrawals; numeric value: 1750.0; detail: A $3.00 surcharge less $1.25 combined venue and upstream shares retains $1.75 per withdrawal. Four thousand annual withdrawals retain $7,000 before operator servicing expenses.

text.title: Assumptions: Card examples assume a $50 average ticket. Gateway yield is a separate component, not an additional merchant cohort. ATM events are withdrawals, not purchases; differing event economics prevent direct conclusions about account profitability. Bars are not additive.
